title: The World Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The World upright: completion, wholeness; reversed: loose ends. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it for your question.
image_alt: The World, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a dancer wrapped in a scarf holds a wand in each hand inside an oval laurel wreath, with a human head, an eagle, a bull and a lion in the corners.
capsule: The World, card XXI and the last of the Major Arcana, stands for completion, fulfillment and accomplishment. Reversed, it shows something almost finished, with loose ends still open. It is a good card that asks you to notice how far you have come. A closed circle with a free dancer inside answers yes when the card is upright.

blocks.heading: What is on The World card?
paragraphs: A tall oval wreath fills most of the card, and inside it a figure dances in midair. Waite describes "an elliptic garland, as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things" (p. 30). On the 1909 card the wreath is green and leafy, bound with red ribbons at the top and bottom, set against a pale blue sky, with XXI printed above.

The dancer is, in Waite's words, a woman "whom the wind has girt about the loins with a light scarf, and this is all her vesture"; he adds: "She is in the act of dancing, and has a wand in either hand" (p. 30). On the 1909 card the scarf is a long gray-violet band winding around her body, and both wands are white.

Heads look out from clouds in the four corners: on the 1909 card, a human head and an eagle above, a bull and a lion below. Waite calls them "the four living creatures of the Apocalypse and Ezekiel's vision" and notes that Christian symbolism assigns them to the evangelists (p. 30).

He reads the dance as "the swirl of the sensitive life" and "joy attained in the body" (p. 30). In Part II he did not describe the picture again, because its design is "unchanged—and indeed unchangeable" (p. 156).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The World?
paragraphs: The upright list joins two ideas: reward for something done, and movement to a new place, by road or abroad. The reversed list turns both into stillness, things that stay fixed and do not move on. Arcana Diary takes the first as recognition of what you have done, not as a promise of results.

Waite calls the card "this final message of the Major Trumps" and says it represents "the perfection and end of the Cosmos" (p. 156). He also reports that Éliphas Lévi called the garland a crown (pp. 30–31).

blocks.heading: What does The World mean upright?
paragraphs: Completion is the core of The World: a cycle coming together, a piece of work finished, a stage of life that now makes sense as a whole. It is accomplishment you can feel inside, not only the kind other people see. It is also the card of success and celebration, of a milestone reached and marked, and often of travel or a wider world opening up.

Wholeness and integration are its deeper side. What you learned along the way fits together, and you feel at home in yourself. The dancer is not grasping at anything; the wreath around her is already closed.

Waite's list adds movement and a change of place; that an ending here prepares the next start is a modern reading, not Waite's. Take a moment to honor how much you have grown before you open the next chapter.

blocks.heading: What does The World mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The World points to something almost finished but not quite closed: a last step that keeps getting put off, a lack of closure that leaves you hovering between what was and what comes next. It can also stand for delays, or for shortcuts that reach the end faster but leave the result unfinished.

Waite's reversed words, inertia, fixity, stagnation and permanence, describe that same stuck place from outside: nothing moves. The last step that keeps getting put off belongs to the modern reading, not to Waite.
Find the loose ends and tie off just one of them; a single closed thread can make the rest feel lighter.

blocks.heading: What does The World mean in love?
paragraphs: Feeling whole in yourself comes first with The World, and from there closeness can feel like sharing rather than needing. For anyone unattached, that can mean a contentment that does not depend on finding someone.

Inside a couple, the card can mark a fulfilling, committed relationship, often at a milestone, with a sense of fit and of having grown through something side by side, and room left to keep growing. A small celebration of what you have built suits it well.
Something left unsaid or unfinished on your side, or a feeling that a piece is still missing, may be keeping a chapter open when the card is reversed; look for it.

blocks.heading: What does The World mean for work and money?
paragraphs: The World at work is about arrival: wrapping up a project, completing a course, reaching the point where your effort adds up. It favors ending things properly: a summary, a thank-you, a pause before the next task.
For money, The World is a goal reached: a target met, long effort finally adding up to stability, the sense of having built something solid.
With the card reversed, find the single unfinished step that holds everything else in place.

blocks.heading: What is The World's advice?
paragraphs: Finish one small task you left almost done and mark it complete. Closing the circle on purpose stops it tugging at you. Cross it off, say it out loud, and let yourself feel the click of something finished.

blocks.heading: Is The World a yes or no card?
The World as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: The World's figure is someone at ease in their own skin, who has come through a long stretch and carries it lightly; in you, it is the self that feels complete. Feelings under The World are settled: love that feels whole and committed, quiet satisfaction with the bond, a sense that the relationship fits. Reversed, the feelings are there but not fully settled: a restless almost-there, something still missing, a closure not yet reached or a hesitation to commit completely.

pairs.text: An ending and a new start touch. Close this chapter clearly, then begin the next with curiosity.
Completion at home and among your people. Enjoy the belonging you helped build.
One goal reached, a wider view ahead. Look at what this finish makes possible.
Long practice bears fruit. Recognize the skill you built step by step.

blocks.heading: The World or the Wheel of Fortune?
paragraphs: The Wheel of Fortune also has four creatures in its corners; Waite notes that "the four Living Creatures of Ezekiel occupy the angles of the card" (p. 108). Today the Wheel is read as cycles and change, a turning point in motion. The World is the circle at rest: a cycle completed rather than still turning. If everything is shifting, think of the Wheel; if something has come together, The World.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The World
paragraphs: What have I finished recently that I have not let myself acknowledge?
Which loose end is still keeping a chapter open?
What did I learn in this cycle that I want to carry into the next one?

faq.q: Is The World a good or bad card?
faq.a: A good card, and a satisfying one to draw. It backs completion, a sense of wholeness and credit for what you have done. Reversed, an unfinished end can keep you from enjoying the result, so tying it off matters more than reaching perfection.

It can be read that way. Waite's list includes voyage, route, emigration and change of place (p. 287), so movement is part of the old meaning. On Arcana Diary that movement is read more widely: a move into a new stage, with or without a suitcase.

faq.q: Is The World the last card of the tarot?
faq.a: It is the last of the Major Arcana, number XXI. Waite wrote that he took care "not to number the World or Universe otherwise than as 21" (p. 161). The 56 cards of the Minor Arcana follow as a separate group of four suits.

faq.q: Who is the dancer on The World card?
faq.a: Waite calls her simply a woman, wearing only a scarf (p. 30). He reports that Éliphas Lévi saw her as Truth, and adds that Truth belongs more properly to the seventeenth card (pp. 31, 159). Read today, she can be anyone who feels at home in their own life.

waite.quote: Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place. Reversed: Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence.
